solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Number Ten popular after reversing policy at last (6)

indicatorNotes.after: popular comes after ten before the pair is turned round
indicatorNotes.reversing: the pair TEN IN is turned back to front
indicatorNotes.at last: take only the final letter of policy

blocks.note: the number written as a word

annotation.surface: A political sketch: Downing Street's standing rises after a U-turn on policy.
annotation.walkthrough: Number Ten looks like Downing Street, but 'Number' is the definition and 'Ten' is just TEN, joined by IN and flipped to NINET.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain definition by category: ninety is one particular number, the kind of broad class-word setters often use for numerals.

entries.clue: Liberal supporting opera – typical! (6)

indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down answer, a supporting piece sits underneath the one it holds up

annotation.surface: A weary sigh that a Liberal would, predictably, back the opera.
annotation.walkthrough: Norma is a Bellini opera, a crossword favourite because its name hides so many words.
annotation.definitionFit: Normal and typical both mean usual or standard.

entries.clue: Snapper we arranged for The Telegraph? (9)

indicatorNotes.arranged: the letters are put into a new order

annotation.surface: A photographer asks whether a shoot was set up for the paper itself.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is by example, flagged by the question mark: The Telegraph is one newspaper, and the one printing this very puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: The Telegraph is one British daily, and the one printing this puzzle.

entries.clue: Storm split a party (7)

annotation.surface: A political row: a storm splits a party down the middle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Split a party' reads as a verb phrase about a political row; here split is the adjective TORN.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific for a general: a twister is one violent, whirling kind of storm.

entries.clue: Remembered name adopted by grass (8)

indicatorNotes.adopted by: the grass takes the name into itself

blocks.note: a reed is a tall grass

annotation.surface: A plant whose remembered name was taken on by a grass.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Name adopted' suggests a new surname, as in adoption; here adopted means taken in, so the grass wraps around the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: To recall something is to remember it.

entries.clue: Regular type of rugby not using wings (4)

indicatorNotes.not using wings: the wings of a word are its two end letters, which are dropped

blocks.note: drop the first and last letters of sEVENs

annotation.surface: A rugby variant played without wingers.
annotation.walkthrough: Sevens is the seven-a-side form of rugby; 'wings' looks like positions on the pitch but means the word's outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a steady, unvarying pulse or rhythm can be called either regular or even.

entries.clue: Country song about just leaving Jack (7)

indicatorNotes.about: the song goes around the other piece
indicatorNotes.leaving: J for Jack departs from JUST

blocks.note: an aria is an operatic song

annotation.surface: A country song about someone who has just walked out on Jack.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country song' reads as one phrase, a genre of music; split it, and Country is the definition and song is ARIA. J = Jack, as on playing cards.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Alpine republic, capital Vienna, is one nation among many.

entries.clue: Row over new fabric (5)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down answer, the first piece sits on top of the second

annotation.surface: An argument over a new fabric.
annotation.walkthrough: Row reads as a quarrel, but it is the kind of row you stand in.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: cloth woven from flax is one kind of fabric.

entries.clue: Swimmers note records broken by China endlessly (8)

indicatorNotes.broken by: the records are split open and something put inside
indicatorNotes.endlessly: China loses both its end letters

blocks.note: do (doh), a note of the sol-fa scale

annotation.surface: Swimmers setting records, with China nearly ending their run.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a swimming gala, with China as a rival nation; the swimmers are marine ones.
annotation.definitionFit: Dolphins are swimming marine mammals.

entries.clue: Profit from revolutionary magnet, perhaps? (6)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution turns the word round

blocks.note: a magnet draws things to it, so it is a drawer

annotation.surface: Making money out of a new kind of magnet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' warns of a whimsical definition: a magnet is something that draws, a drawer, not the kind in a desk.
annotation.definitionFit: A reward is a profit or return for something done.

entries.clue: Romeo, young man wearing ring in private (8)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the ring goes around Romeo and the young man, as clothes surround a wearer

blocks.note: a peal is a ring of bells
R is Romeo in the NATO alphabet
a son is a young man

annotation.surface: Romeo and a young man exchange rings in secret.
annotation.walkthrough: Ring looks like jewellery on a wedding finger; it is the sound of bells, a PEAL.
annotation.definitionFit: Personal and private both mean belonging to one person, not public.

entries.clue: A playful seal pup’s clapping (8)

indicatorNotes.playful: the letters play about into a new order

annotation.surface: A frolicking young seal flapping its flippers together.
annotation.walkthrough: Seals really are known for clapping their flippers, so the surface picture and the answer meet.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an audience's clapping of hands is the commonest form of approval it gives.

entries.clue: Crush culinary vegetable (6)

blocks.note: a gourd such as butternut or acorn

annotation.surface: A cook mashing vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one kitchen instruction, but it is two separate meanings of SQUASH side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: to press something flat, and the family of gourds such as butternut cooked as vegetables.

entries.clue: Bishop was in charge of church subdivision (6)

blocks.note: B = bishop, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A bishop who oversaw part of a church's organisation.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes one church body of it; church is only CH, and subdivision stands alone.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a local office or division of a bank, shop chain or society is one part of the whole.

entries.clue: Difficulty in fight with European (6)

annotation.surface: Trouble in a brawl involving a European.
annotation.walkthrough: Fight and difficulty sit so close that the whole clue reads as one scuffle; fight is only SCRAP, a British word for a brawl.
annotation.definitionFit: A scrape is a difficult or awkward situation.

entries.clue: An opinion broadcast with curt way of speaking (13)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: the letters are scattered and re-sown

annotation.surface: A pundit voices a view on air in a clipped manner.
annotation.walkthrough: Broadcast suggests radio, and curt suggests a manner of speech, but curt is only four letters to mix in.
annotation.definitionFit: Pronunciation is the way a word or language is spoken.

entries.clue: Looked closely at centipedes lacking energy to run (9)

indicatorNotes.lacking: one E for energy is removed
indicatorNotes.to run: the remaining letters run into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone peers at centipedes too sluggish to scurry off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lacking energy to run' reads as a tired centipede; E = energy, and run is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: examining something carefully for faults, as an official might, is looking closely at it.

entries.clue: Maybe Glaswegian periodically learns to conserve old vehicles (8)

indicatorNotes.Maybe: a Glaswegian is one example of a Scot
indicatorNotes.periodically: periodically means at regular intervals, so letters are taken at regular spacing through the word
indicatorNotes.to conserve: the pieces keep O safe inside them

annotation.surface: A thrifty Glaswegian learns to preserve his old cars.
annotation.walkthrough: Glaswegian is from Glasgow, Scotland's largest city; O sits between SCO and T.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: mopeds and kick-along two-wheelers are kinds of vehicle.

entries.clue: Scans cut crime, bizarre state of affairs (13)

indicatorNotes.bizarre: the letters come out in a strange order

annotation.surface: A headline: scanning has reduced crime, which is odd.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma splits a news headline from a comment, but 'bizarre' belongs to the wordplay and the definition is the last three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Circumstances are the conditions or state of affairs around something.

entries.clue: Upper-class university admitting group of students nearly all odd (7)

indicatorNotes.admitting: the two U's let the students in between them

blocks.note: the NUS is the National Union of Students

annotation.surface: An elite university that takes in almost every student group.
annotation.walkthrough: The NUS is the UK's National Union of Students. 'Upper-class university' reads as one place, but it is two separate U's.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something odd is out of the ordinary, strange or rare.

entries.clue: Bewilder Conservative and join (7)

annotation.surface: A Tory recruitment pitch: join up and be baffled.
annotation.walkthrough: Con is the standard short form of Conservative, the British party also called the Tories.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to leave someone puzzled and unable to think clearly.

entries.clue: Edgings from clothier adorned large bed (6)

indicatorNotes.Edgings from: the edges of each word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of ClothieR
first and last letters of AdorneD
first and last letters of LargE

annotation.surface: A tailor's trimmings used to decorate a big bed.
annotation.walkthrough: Edgings sounds like fabric trim, which suits the clothier; here it means the edges of the three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a rocking cot for an infant is one kind of bed.

entries.clue: Amount produced in unfashionable place (6)

annotation.surface: Production figures from some unfashionable town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unfashionable place' reads as a noun phrase, but place is the verb PUT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a factory's production over a period is measured as its yield.

entries.clue: Some other extremely comforting word (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: only part of the letters that follow is taken

annotation.surface: Another very reassuring thing to say.
annotation.walkthrough: 'There, there' is what you say to comfort someone, which makes the definition fair.
annotation.definitionFit: "There" is said to soothe someone, as in "there, there".

entries.clue: Antlered animals in river run after drained relative (8)

indicatorNotes.after: the pieces before it follow the drained relative
indicatorNotes.drained: relative is emptied of its middle, leaving the outer letters

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Britain
R = run, as on a cricket scoresheet

annotation.surface: Deer wading into a river after a relative has been drained.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word joining definition to wordplay, but it is a piece; the Dee is a river in Scotland and Wales.
annotation.definitionFit: Reindeer are deer, and both sexes grow antlers.

entries.clue: Observed part of play, we hear (4)

indicatorNotes.we hear: the answer sounds like the wordplay when spoken

blocks.note: a scene is part of a play

annotation.surface: A remark that part of a play has reportedly been watched.
annotation.walkthrough: A scene is a section of a play's act; said out loud it matches the past participle of see.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are past participles meaning noticed or witnessed with the eyes.

entries.clue: Did former English copper start to threaten editor? (8)

indicatorNotes.start to: take the first letter of threaten

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

annotation.surface: A question about whether a retired English policeman began threatening a newspaper editor.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper looks like a policeman, and Did like the auxiliary starting a question; Did is the definition, and copper is the metal Cu.
annotation.definitionFit: To execute a task is to do it, so executed means did.

entries.clue: Dressed up, took court action to protect it (6)

indicatorNotes.to protect: the court action surrounds IT, guarding it

blocks.note: to sue is to take court action

annotation.surface: Someone put on their best suit to go to court and defend it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone dressing for court, which is exactly where the SUED comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Clothes-based sense: wearing a formal jacket and trousers, as in suited and booted, is being dressed up.

entries.clue: Island group handles closure of airport badly (8)

indicatorNotes.closure of: the close of a word is its last letter
indicatorNotes.badly: the letters are put into a poor order

annotation.surface: Islanders cope poorly with their airport being shut.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a news story about an island airport shutting; closure means the end letter. Shetland is a group of islands north of Scotland.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this archipelago north of mainland Scotland is one island group.

entries.clue: Annoy weak-kneed leftie, to an extent (6)

indicatorNotes.to an extent: only part of the words is used

annotation.surface: A jibe at a spineless left-winger, only partly meant.
annotation.walkthrough: Leftie is British slang for a left-winger.
annotation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: jabbing at someone with sharp remarks, as a sewing point would, irritates them.
